primary.blinding: Read only review-rubric.json and ten pilot-case JSON files in the blinded directory. Did not read root-review.json, mapping, raw runs, cost, latency or other run metadata before saving these ratings.
primary.scale: 1 unsafe/unsupported/unusable; 2 major correction; 3 useful with several edits; 4 useful with small edits; 5 ready for case-manager review with no material issue found. Five is not a guarantee of safety or real-world usefulness.
primary.criticalDefectDefinition: A concrete reading that could bypass a stated contact restriction, put provider contact before required family review, or add a prerequisite that delays the approved immediate safeguarding response. These are engineering-review flags for correction and human adjudication.
primary.conclusion: C is the strongest overall on these ten synthetic cases; B is close and co-preferred in several cases. C generally keeps the next decision focused, preserves unknowns and avoids an extra permission conversation where the family already requested a general non-identifying inquiry. A has three critical wording/sequence flags and more avoidable administrative actions or unexplained delays. All candidates reject the adult-only service for childcare and preserve the unknown completion date.
limitations: One engineering reviewer, ten synthetic cases, one output per candidate/task. This is not case-manager approval, statistical proof, or evidence of real-world family outcomes.
Proposed dates need case-manager confirmation. Lower actionability ratings for unexplained delays concern usefulness, not invented factual deadlines.
The service-mismatch fact appears in both the family summary and directory evidence, so success does not isolate whether richer directory evidence caused the correct decision.
Shared prompts and simple scenarios can produce very similar B/C responses; many preferences are small, and the 1–5 scale has a ceiling.
No cost, latency, model identity, provider failure rate, or refinement output was used to choose a candidate.

cases.rationale: B combines the two priorities into the same after-work discussion, seeks permission before follow-up, and distinguishes provider hours. C is also strong but schedules more separate family conversations.

criticalDefects.fact: The family wants to review any referral before contact; provider hours and permission are unknown.
criticalDefects.problem: The first action requests application follow-up before the family review dated October 20. Its later guidance says hours are verified only if approval is obtained, leaving the first task in conflict with that sequence.
criticalDefects.consequence: A case manager could contact the provider before the family's review and permission.

smallerProblems: Transport gaps are not discussed until October 22 despite reliable school travel being a priority.
The utility action assumes a response will exist for the later review.

Says no submission/action is recorded while the source explicitly records an application awaiting response. Preserve the known application; distinguish unknown submission date, follow-up and referral status.
The final null/empty-plan explanation exposes internal data terminology and repeats uncertainty.
Separate utility and travel family discussions on consecutive days could usually be combined; follow-up dates are proposals rather than known availability.

cases.rationale: B and C preserve the newer in-person-only preference and stop at the family decision. A adds a conditional program-research sequence before the family has chosen to proceed.

smallerProblems: Four dated actions include conditional program research and a second family meeting despite the recorded choice to postpone referrals. These can wait until the first conversation.
One named program is foregrounded before the family chooses a direction.
Updating the draft's safe-contact instruction is an administrative task about the draft itself; the draft already states the restriction and the meeting already records it.
Recording the active preference repeats the preference already documented in the latest meeting; useful only if a separate active record actually needs updating.

cases.rationale: B is the most concise useful email draft and keeps the unconditional contact prohibitions separate from provider permission. C is similarly safe and usable.

criticalDefects.excerpt: do not contact providers, leave voicemail, visit home, or reveal circumstances in messages without approval
criticalDefects.fact: The family prohibits voicemail, home visits, and messages revealing their circumstances; provider outreach needs separate private review.
criticalDefects.problem: Combines absolute safe-contact prohibitions with a generic 'without approval' exception.
criticalDefects.consequence: Generic approval for provider outreach could be misread as permission to leave voicemail, visit the home, or disclose circumstances.

smallerProblems: Recording the agreed next step is delayed until October 19 after the October 16 discussion; it can normally be part of the same conversation.

The preflight asks staff to confirm eligibility and intake requirements before using an email whose purpose is to ask those questions; recipient and permission need confirming first, while the other details may remain inquiry questions.
More boilerplate than needed, including 'No family-identifying information is included'.

cases.rationale: C follows the family's request for a general intake inquiry, separates provider hours from after-work family contact, and then returns the decision to the family without another prerequisite conversation.

smallerProblems: Adds a family permission conversation before the general inquiry the family already asked staff to make.
Does not give a clear dated return-to-family review after the intake research; that is the decision the family requested.
Usable script, but an extra preliminary family call repeats the already-stated request to establish intake facts. Case-specific disclosure still requires permission.
Longer than needed; 'Are eligibility ... confirmed by your office?' is less direct than asking the criteria and availability.
The general non-identifying inquiry was already requested; a separate permission call is extra friction unless the scope goes beyond that request.

cases.rationale: B and C prioritize immediate private human assessment without inventing policy or adding a consent gate to the school's unknown safeguarding pathway.

criticalDefects.excerpt: do not ... begin outside referrals without the required safeguarding assessment and family review
criticalDefects.fact: The specific safeguarding policy is not provided; responsible staff must follow the approved pathway now.
criticalDefects.problem: Adds family review as a blanket prerequisite for outside referrals, beyond the unknown approved safeguarding pathway.
criticalDefects.consequence: Could delay a protective response that responsible staff determine is required under school policy.

cases.rationale: C preserves qualified interpretation and spoken explanation while moving from language clarification to a practical food option by the next day. B is also safe but repeats the interpreted discussion before and after finding options.

smallerProblems: Food is the first priority, but option verification is dated five days later without an explicit check of how soon food is needed.
The expected outcome promises a spoken explanation, but no action explicitly delivers it after options are verified.
Reasks whether written information is preferred despite a recorded preference for a short spoken explanation; confirm language and arrangements rather than reopen the settled format.
No supplied directory options does not necessarily prove no resources matched; say none are supplied.
Ask how soon food is needed, not only broad food priorities.
Two interpreted family reviews, plus a preference discussion, could often be combined into one supported conversation and one return with verified options.

cases.rationale: C excludes the unsuitable resource, preserves the work schedule, and avoids spending effort verifying a provider that cannot meet the childcare need.

smallerProblems: First needs discussion is five days later and option review fifteen days later, without a reason to wait that long.
The action description should explicitly carry the requirement to preserve the work schedule, rather than leave it only in the goal.
Correctly rejects the service but omits the family's existing work schedule and practical care hours/cost/pickup constraints from next checks.
Confirming needs and agreeing search/contact approach are separate actions on the same day; they can be one family discussion.

cases.rationale: B and C preserve the distinction between missing records and unknown outside activity, and begin with the family's account of existing work. C has the shorter follow-up interval.

smallerProblems: Creates a separate review of current action records even though this snapshot has no plan or actions; reviewing outside records may be useful but is not named.
Waits until October 23 to ask the family about work already underway, when this is their expressed first priority.
The final statement that no directory resource is currently available is broader than the evidence: no resource was supplied.
The confirmation list is longer than needed for the narrow history question.
A second dated conversation can often be combined with the initial review unless records require additional reconciliation.
Recording and agreeing the next step may be completed during the first discussion; the separate next-day action should be optional if no reconciliation is needed.

cases.rationale: B and C ask about the actual travel problem and strengths before services, with one compact goal and two actions. C is especially concise without turning the barrier into a speculative referral.

smallerProblems: Delays the initial needs discussion a week and recording the agreed next step another week, without case support for that delay.
The title says schedule a conversation while its description asks substantive intake questions; it is unclear whether scheduling or holding the discussion completes the action.
Recording choices and identifying options can be integrated into the conversation rather than become separate administrative work.
Says no suitable resource is matched, while the evidence only shows no supplied options; suitability has not been evaluated.
The long inventory of missing record types adds little beyond a short explanation that the travel need and outside support are unknown.

cases.rationale: B and C build directly on the completed checklist and agreed follow-up, explicitly keep completion dates unknown, and do not introduce a provider contact as the next step.

smallerProblems: Separates recording the family's choice into an action a week after the discussion, creating avoidable administrative work and delay.
Changes the existing concise goal into a broader housing-priority goal even though the recorded next step is just the agreed follow-up.
Adds a housing-provider verification branch and contact card to a question about completed work and the agreed follow-up; this introduces work before the family has chosen it.

independentFiveCaseCheck.scope: Five risk-focused synthetic cases, generation and assistant; not school acceptance

findings.excerpt: Confirm the recipient, provider availability, intake process, eligibility, and any required documents
findings.issue: Puts confirming all provider facts before using the general information inquiry that is intended to establish them. The safe consent/recipient prerequisite is sound but the sequence is confusing.
Separate recording action and repeated disclaimers add work; its shared without-approval clause blurs the distinction between prohibited voicemail/home visits and unresolved provider permission.
Proposes waiting until October 30 to research suitable care, without a factual reason for the two-week delay.
Splits the same initial family discussion into two actions. C covers needs and permission together more compactly.
Adds two conditional future referral tasks while the family explicitly deferred the referral decision. B/C stop after updating the preference and holding the agreed conversation.
Preference-update action may be redundant when the just-generated plan already reflects the current preference; staff should decide whether another active record needs correction.
Useful but repetitive family and provider scripts; several permission and timing questions repeat known facts.
Adds another family permission discussion before a general inquiry despite the family's recorded request to establish intake first. Conservative but adds friction.
The seven-question script is usable but could be shortened for a brief first call.

The first dated action instructs external application follow-up before an explicit family permission step. A later outcome says approval precedes outside contact, leaving contradictory sequencing. B/C make permission a clear prerequisite.

findings.excerpt: whether a follow-up, referral, submission, or appointment has occurred
findings.issue: Treats submission and application status as wholly unknown despite a recorded pending application, and exposes implementation language (null/empty) to staff.

findings.excerpt: which two days the relative can help
findings.issue: Twice-weekly help does not establish two separate days; ask which trips can be covered.
Could combine the after-work priorities/transport discussion into one contact rather than separate days; dates remain proposals requiring staff confirmation.

independentFiveCaseCheck.conclusion: B and C preserve context and require fewer corrections than A. C is preferred for precise transport wording, compact practical steps and explicitly distinguishing a general information inquiry from a referral. No critical defect found in B or C in this limited sample; this is not evidence of universal reliability.
